title: AI and Offloading: A Complex Relationship?
author: Marc Smith
summary: Marc Smith uses cognitive psychology research on offloading to ask when and what learners should hand to external tools, and then applies it to AI. He starts from the limits of working memory and shows that people with lower subjective capacity offload sooner, while expecting later access to information, as in the photo-taking impairment and Google effects, weakens recall of the content itself. The second half turns to Daiki Nakamura's augmentation-erosion framework, which separates peripheral cognitive operations that AI can safely take over from constitutive ones where the intended learning actually happens. The same act, such as asking AI to summarise a paper, can therefore help or harm depending on the learning goal. Smith stresses that performance with AI is not learning, and that unaided, delayed assessment is the right test. He closes with four regulation skills for learners and warns of a metacognitive trap in which fluent AI output inflates a sense of understanding.
points: Offloading is a normal way to manage working memory, and learners with lower subjective capacity or heavier load do it sooner, so the real question is what to offload and when.
Expecting later access to information, whether via photos, notes or the internet, tends to reduce memory for the information itself while improving memory for where to find it.
Nakamura's framework separates peripheral operations that AI can take over from constitutive ones that carry the learning, so the same AI request can be augmentation or erosion depending on the goal.
Performance with AI is not learning, which means durable, unaided and ideally delayed assessment is the fair test of whether AI use helped.
Productive AI use needs partition discernment, calibrated monitoring, disciplinary verification and conversion of AI-assisted work into independent skill.
quotes: Working memory is limited in both capacity and duration, which is why we often offload information to external sources (anything from writing a list and jotting down mathematical calculations to storing phone number in our phones).
It appears people are more likely to offload memories of items when they believe they’ll have external access to them later.

AI not only allows us to offload cognition, it also allows us to outsource it, and how and why we do this impacts how and what we learn. There’s a difference, therefore, between cognitive assistance and cognitive substitution.

Erosion is when AI undermines learning by taking over cognitive operations essential to the learning goal. This can potentially prevent the learner from developing and maintaining the relevant knowledge and skills.
According to Nakamura, offloading a constitutive operation need not cause erosion if the learner then engages meaningfully with the AI output or reconstructs the reasoning independently.
ChatGPT might be able to construct a perfect answer to a question, but this tells us little about whether the learner has developed the knowledge needed to produce that answer independently
rather than confusing fluent AI output with their own understanding
There’s also a potential metacognitive trap here. AI-assisted success may produce an exaggerated sense of understanding, leaving learners unaware that their independent capabilities haven’t improved.
